title: jadero.dev v2: plan review
summary: The build plan for jadero.dev v2, a multilingual (es, en, de) portfolio that proves broad engineering skills: backend architecture, reliability and messaging, testing, CI/CD and infrastructure, security, frontend craft, engineering process and applied AI. It supports an internal move to the agentic team and stands equally for any future role. The backend is a modular monolith plus a few services where isolation pays, with RabbitMQ between them, deployed by CI/CD to the owner's Hetzner CX33; the ask-me agent, RAG and MCP work is one strong showcase among those pillars. Each card is one decision with options, trade-offs and a recommendation; full reasoning lives in the ADRs of report.md, and nothing gets built until these are decided (WP-0). Owner review (2026-10-03): all 76 decisions are recorded (55 decided, 21 decided with a change from the owner's notes or the second-pass audit); the open follow-ups were settled in conversation on 2026-10-03 and the plan ships as releases R0 to R7 without dates (owner-review-followups.md, section 6).

decisions.title: Monorepo tooling
decisions.question: Which tool should manage the monorepo that holds every app and shared package?
decisions.context: A monorepo keeps several apps and shared packages in one repository so a contract change and all its consumers ship in one pull request. A monorepo tool understands which package depends on which, so it can run only the tasks affected by a change and cache results it has already computed. Without one, every CI run rebuilds and retests everything.

options.label: Turborepo + pnpm
options.description: pnpm workspaces for packages, Turborepo for the task graph and caching.
pros: pnpm catalogs pin shared versions once
cons: Module boundaries need a separate tool (dependency-cruiser)

options.label: Nx
options.description: A full monorepo platform with generators, a project graph and boundary rules.
cons: Its Nest plugin lags new Nest majors

options.label: pnpm workspaces only
options.description: Just the package manager's workspace feature.
cons: No affected-only CI: everything rebuilds every time

options.label: Separate repos per app
options.description: One repository per deployable.
cons: Agents cannot see both sides of an API change

decisions.why: Turborepo gives caching and affected runs with very little configuration, and pnpm is the fastest, strictest package manager for workspaces. Nx is more than this project needs, plain workspaces waste CI time, and separate repos break shared contracts.
decisions.learn: Task graph, build cache, affected runs, internal packages (compiled vs just-in-time).

decisions.title: Runtime topology and edge
decisions.question: How should traffic reach the services, and where does the admin live?
decisions.context: The edge is the first thing a request hits: it terminates TLS, decides which service gets the request and can apply cross-cutting rules like rate limits and authentication. The server already runs nginx, which can do all of that. Same origin means the browser sees the API on the same domain as the page, so cookies work simply and there is no CORS configuration. The edge component itself is now decided once, in D-45, because the owner noted the overlap; this card keeps the deployables and same origin per audience.

options.label: Host nginx as gateway, same origin per audience
options.description: nginx routes jadero.dev/api/* and admin.jadero.dev/api/* to each service, rate-limits, checks admin sessions with auth_request and serves stale pages if web is down.
cons: Config is not TypeScript (checked with nginx -t in CI)

options.label: Dedicated gateway (Traefik or Kong)
options.description: A container that routes by Docker labels or plugins.
cons: Another process in every request's path

options.label: A NestJS gateway service
options.description: Every request goes through a Nest app that proxies to the others.
cons: Becomes the single point of failure and coupling the service split tries to remove

decisions.why: Same origin per audience keeps cookies first-party and removes CORS entirely. Which component runs the edge (nginx alone, or nginx plus a thin NestJS gateway) is now D-45's question.
decisions.learn: API gateway, gateway offloading, same-origin policy, CORS.
decisions.ownerNote: Repeats D-45. nginx looks simplest, but for learning the owner would like a NestJS gateway service, ideally the best of both; wants to discuss it.
decisions.change: Scope narrowed (F-2): D-2 covers the deployables and same origin per audience (jadero.dev, admin.jadero.dev). The edge component is decided once, in D-45.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: Confirm that D-2 now covers only the deployables and same origin per audience, with the edge component decided once in D-45.

decisions.title: Architecture inside each service
decisions.question: How should code be organized inside each NestJS service?
decisions.context: Layered architecture groups code by technical role (controller, service, repository) and lets business code import the database library directly. Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters) puts business rules in the center and makes them depend only on interfaces (ports); databases and APIs plug in as adapters, so the core can be tested without any infrastructure. Both can be used in the same codebase, module by module.

options.label: Hexagonal where it pays, layered for trivial modules
options.description: Content, auth, knowledge, chat, usage and submissions are hexagonal; health, revalidation and cv stay layered.
pros: Each pattern used where its benefit is visible
Provider switches never touch business code
cons: Two styles to recognize (documented per module)

options.label: Layered everywhere
options.description: Classic Nest structure: controllers call services that call the ORM.
cons: Business code coupled to Drizzle and SDKs
Tests need a database or heavy mocks

options.label: Hexagonal everywhere
options.description: Every module gets domain, application, infrastructure and presentation layers.
cons: Ceremony on modules that only pass data through

decisions.why: Using hexagonal only where there are real rules or external systems shows judgment and keeps the core testable, without adding layers to code that does not need them.
decisions.learn: Ports and adapters, dependency inversion, use case, repository, anti-corruption layer.
decisions.ownerNote: Asks whether more layers make sense: a service as orchestrator, a DAO service for data access, utils, shared modules, and hexagonal ports as abstract classes so adapters follow one shape where it applies.
decisions.change: Layer conventions added to ADR-003: controller, application service as orchestrator, repository for data access; ports as abstract classes used as DI tokens; no generic utils folder; sharing across services only through named infrastructure packages.

decisions.title: NestJS major version
decisions.question: Should the backend start on NestJS 12 (released 2026-08-27) or the mature NestJS 11?
decisions.context: NestJS 12 ships its packages as ECMAScript modules (ESM), validates requests with Standard Schema libraries such as Zod, makes Vitest the default test runner for ESM projects and requires Node 20.19+ or 22.12+. NestJS 11 is the battle-tested line with CommonJS and Jest. Starting on the old major means a migration later; starting on the new one means some third-party modules may lag for a while.

options.label: NestJS 12, ESM, Vitest, Node 22
options.description: Current major, with a compatibility spike in WP-3 before features depend on it.
pros: ESM matches Next and the LangChain packages
cons: Some modules may not declare v12 support yet

options.label: NestJS 11, CommonJS, Jest
options.description: The mature line.
pros: Everything in the ecosystem works today
cons: ESM interop friction with AI packages

decisions.why: A greenfield project should start on the current major; the WP-3 spike catches any incompatible module early, and the fallback is a thin own wrapper rather than a downgrade.
decisions.learn: ESM vs CommonJS, require(esm), Standard Schema.
decisions.ownerNote: Fine to use NestJS 12 although work uses older versions; learning it here gives data to propose the version bump at work.

decisions.title: Database access (ORM)
decisions.question: Which library should services use to talk to Postgres?
decisions.context: An ORM or query builder maps database tables to TypeScript types and builds queries. This project needs pgvector columns and indexes for the agent and plain relational tables for content, and the owner wants to learn SQL rather than hide it. Migrations (versioned schema changes) should be reviewable SQL.

options.label: Drizzle ORM
options.description: TypeScript schema, SQL-like queries, generated SQL migrations.
pros: Native vector columns, HNSW indexes and distance helpers
cons: No official Nest module (a small own provider)

options.label: Prisma
options.description: Schema DSL with a generated client.
cons: Prisma 7 treats vector as Unsupported (raw SQL)
Prisma 8 is a release candidate with breaking moves

options.label: TypeORM
options.description: Decorator-based entities.

options.label: Kysely or raw pg
options.description: A typed query builder or plain driver.

decisions.why: Drizzle supports pgvector natively and keeps SQL visible, which matches both the agent's needs and the learning goal. Prisma is mid-transition, and TypeORM teaches nothing new.
decisions.learn: Schema migrations, query builders, repository pattern, transactions.
decisions.ownerNote: Has used Prisma and TypeORM; Drizzle is now in use at work, so the owner wants to learn it.

decisions.title: Validation and shared contracts
decisions.question: How should request, response and event data be validated and shared between apps?
decisions.context: Every boundary (HTTP request, event, environment variable, agent tool input) needs validation so bad data fails early with a clear error. Zod lets you write one schema and get both runtime validation and the TypeScript type. NestJS 12 can now validate requests directly with Zod through Standard Schema.

options.label: Zod via Standard Schema in a shared contracts package
options.description: One schema per DTO or event in packages/contracts, used by forms, services and agent tools.
pros: One schema language end to end
Same schemas generate the OpenAPI document
cons: OpenAPI generation from Zod may need a bridge (verify)

options.label: class-validator DTO classes
options.description: Nest's classic decorator-based validation.
cons: Classes cannot be shared with the browser cleanly
Duplicate schemas for forms and tools

decisions.why: A single Zod schema per contract removes drift between the admin forms, the services, the events and the agent tools.
decisions.learn: Validation at boundaries, contracts, RFC 9457 problem details.
decisions.ownerNote: Generating OpenAPI documentation automatically for every DTO and endpoint contract matters; the owner works on this at work too and wants to learn it well.
decisions.change: OpenAPI generated from the Zod contracts (@nestjs/swagger 12 standardSchemaConverter with zod-openapi), a docs UI outside production and a breaking-change check in CI; new learning WP-51.

decisions.title: Runtime secrets
decisions.question: Where should production secrets (API keys, passwords) live?
decisions.context: A secret's blast radius is everything that can read it. If CI can read production keys, a leaked CI token leaks production. Keeping runtime secrets only on the server, and giving CI only low-limit keys of its own, keeps the blast radius small.

options.label: On the server only
options.description: A .env file per service and environment, mode 600, loaded by compose; CI never sees runtime secrets.
cons: Rotating a key is a manual step on the server (runbook)

options.label: GitHub secrets written at deploy
options.description: CI pushes secrets to the server on every deploy.
cons: CI can read every production secret
Environment secrets need a public repo or paid plan

options.label: SOPS + age
options.description: Encrypted .env files in the repo, decrypted on the server.
cons: Key management to learn on day one

options.label: Server only, sourced from 1Password
options.description: A personal 1Password vault and a read-only service account; templates with op:// references in the repo; the deploy script renders each service's .env with op inject.
pros: Rotation is change it and redeploy
A lost server does not lose the secrets
A tool the owner already uses
cons: A paid 1Password plan if not already owned
Service-account rate limits below Business plans

decisions.why: Recommendation changed from a to d after the owner's note (F-5): 1Password keeps runtime secrets off GitHub as a does, and adds easy rotation and recovery after a server loss; a stays right if the owner has no personal 1Password account.
decisions.learn: Blast radius, least privilege, fail-fast configuration.
decisions.ownerNote: Asks whether 1Password, whose CLI the owner uses lately for secrets, could be an option.
decisions.previousWhy: Server-only secrets are the simplest safe default; SOPS stays available as an optional later work package (WP-34).
decisions.change: Owner has or will create a personal 1Password account (never the employer's). WP-8 installs the op CLI and the read-only service-account token on the server; WP-9 renders each service's .env with op inject from infra/env/<service>.env.tpl before docker compose up. WP-34 (SOPS) is superseded.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: Use a personal 1Password vault as the source of the server's secrets (d), or keep plain server-only files (a)?

decisions.title: Admin authentication
decisions.question: How should the owner log in to the admin?
decisions.context: There is exactly one admin user. A session is a random id stored server-side and sent as an httpOnly cookie; a JWT is a signed token the client holds, which is harder to revoke and easy to leak if stored in browser storage. OAuth lets GitHub prove who you are, so the app never stores a password.

options.label: Better Auth with GitHub OAuth allow-list
options.description: Database sessions, only one allow-listed GitHub user id, CSRF protection, audit log, passkey later.

options.label: Hand-rolled password + TOTP sessions
options.description: argon2id hashes, TOTP second factor, own session table.

options.label: Passport + JWT
options.description: Access and refresh tokens.
cons: Wrong tool for a single-user, same-origin app

options.label: Network-only (Tailscale) without app auth
options.description: Admin reachable only over the private network.
cons: One proxy mistake exposes an open admin

decisions.why: OAuth with an allow-listed immutable user id and server-side sessions is the safe modern default for one user; hand-rolling is the classic place for subtle bugs, and JWT does not fit this shape.
decisions.learn: Sessions vs tokens, OAuth authorization code + PKCE, cookie flags, CSRF.

decisions.title: Testing strategy and coverage
decisions.question: What testing layers and coverage targets should the project enforce?
decisions.context: A test pyramid has many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against real infrastructure and a few end-to-end tests. Fake adapters let business logic run in milliseconds, while Testcontainers starts a real Postgres or RabbitMQ in Docker for integration tests. Contract tests check that every adapter (and every event consumer) honors the same expectations.

options.label: Pyramid + contract suites + Testcontainers, with targets
options.description: Unit tests with fakes, contract suites per port and per event, integration on real Postgres and RabbitMQ; 90% lines and 85% branches on domain and application, 80% per service.
cons: Fakes and contract suites are code to maintain

options.label: Mostly end-to-end tests
options.description: Boot everything and test through HTTP.

options.label: Unit tests with mocks only
options.description: Mock every dependency.
cons: SQL and broker behavior never tested

decisions.why: Fakes keep most tests fast and meaningful, Testcontainers proves the SQL and messaging really work, and contract tests stop services from breaking each other.
decisions.learn: Test pyramid, test doubles, contract testing, Testcontainers, coverage vs correctness.
decisions.ownerNote: As much testing as possible; the server has the resources; asks how all of it fits into GitHub Actions, or whether it needs to.

decisions.title: Observability
decisions.question: How should logs, metrics and traces be collected across services?
decisions.context: Logs say what happened, metrics say how much, traces say where time went across services. With several services and a broker, a single user action crosses many processes, so a trace id must travel in HTTP headers and in message headers to stitch the story together. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for producing that data.

options.label: pino logs + OpenTelemetry to a free hosted tier
options.description: Structured logs with trace ids, OTel traces and metrics exported over OTLP, trace context propagated through RabbitMQ, per-service health, dead-letter alerts.
cons: Telemetry leaves the server (no visitor data in spans)

options.label: Logs + Uptime Kuma only
options.description: JSON logs and uptime checks.
cons: No way to follow a request across services

options.label: Self-hosted Grafana stack
options.description: Loki, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana on the box.
cons: Over 1 GB RAM and real operations work on an 8 GB server

decisions.why: Distributed tracing becomes essential once there are services and a broker, and a free hosted backend gives it without eating the server's memory.
decisions.learn: Three signals, W3C traceparent, context propagation, health checks.

decisions.title: Content management approach
decisions.question: How should site content be stored and edited?
decisions.context: MDX files in the repo make git the CMS but need a deploy per edit. Payload is a full CMS inside Next.js that the owner already knows. An own content module in NestJS is the most work but is the backend showcase, and its content can be shaped for the agent. MDX compiles to JavaScript, so MDX stored in a database is code execution; Markdown with a fixed set of safe directives is not.

options.label: Own NestJS content module + admin app, Markdown bodies
options.description: Aggregates, translations, revisions, publish workflow, events; bodies in sanitized Markdown.

options.label: Payload CMS
options.description: CMS inside the Next app with admin UI and localization.

options.label: MDX in the repo
options.description: Content as files, git as CMS.

decisions.why: The own module is the part of the backend a reviewer will read, and it produces exactly the structured content the agent needs; Markdown keeps rich formatting without executing content.
decisions.learn: Aggregates, translation tables, revisions, publish state machine.
decisions.ownerNote: Asks whether Astro would make sense for the admin; frontend matters little to the owner.

decisions.title: Reliable asynchronous work
decisions.question: How should a service reliably tell other services that something happened?
decisions.context: The dual-write problem: if a service saves data and then crashes before sending the message, other services never find out. The transactional outbox fixes it by writing the message into the same database transaction as the data, then a relay publishes it to the broker. Because the relay may publish twice after a crash, consumers record processed message ids (an inbox) so duplicates are harmless.

options.label: Outbox per service + relay to RabbitMQ + idempotent consumers
options.description: Outbox rows commit with the change; a relay publishes with confirms; consumers dedupe by event id; retry tiers and dead-letter queues.
pros: No broker in the request path
cons: A second or two of latency

options.label: Publish right after commit
options.description: Send the message in the request after saving.
cons: A broker outage breaks user requests

options.label: Outbox + pg-boss
options.description: A Postgres-based queue shared by producer and consumers.
cons: Services would share a database, breaking their isolation

decisions.why: The outbox plus idempotent consumers is the standard way to get reliable messaging between services that each own their database.
decisions.learn: Dual-write problem, transactional outbox, at-least-once delivery, idempotent consumer, dead-letter queue.
decisions.ownerNote: Asks whether a transaction with try/catch and rollback gives atomicity, whether a small database for dead letters makes sense for audit and manual recovery, and suggests tracking events, successes and failures in the admin.
decisions.change: Adds a dead_letters archive table in each service's own database, an admin Events page (outbox, inbox, retries, dead letters) and a replay action; new WP-50. A shared database for dead letters was not used, to keep database per service.

decisions.title: Provider-agnostic AI layer
decisions.question: How should the code stay independent of which AI provider is used for chat, embeddings, reranking and guard checks?
decisions.context: Ports and adapters means the core code depends on an interface (a port) and each provider gets an adapter that implements it, chosen by configuration. LangChain already ships interfaces for chat models and embeddings, but its embeddings interface does not know a model's identity or vector dimension, so nothing would stop mixing vectors from two models in one index. Vectors from different embedding models are not comparable, so switching embedding provider always means re-embedding everything.

options.label: Hybrid: own ports where we own an invariant, LangChain's chat model as the chat port
options.description: Own EmbeddingsPort (with model id and dimension), RerankerPort, KnowledgeIndexPort, GuardClassifierPort; LangChain BaseChatModel for chat; config-driven factory; vector(1024) + index_version + blue-green re-index.
cons: Two styles of port to explain

options.label: Own ports for everything
options.description: Own LlmPort too, with adapters over raw vendor SDKs.
cons: Re-implements tool calling and streaming per provider

options.label: LangChain abstractions as the ports
options.description: BaseChatModel, Embeddings, VectorStore everywhere.

decisions.why: Own the port where the domain has rules (embedding identity, index versions, reranking); reuse LangChain where it already does the hard, non-transferable work (tool calling and streaming across providers).
decisions.learn: Ports and adapters, abstract factory, strategy, blue-green re-index, expand/contract, contract tests.
decisions.ownerNote: Embeddings should be one fixed provider choice, since changing them changes ingestion and vectors cannot be mixed; the movable part is the chat model per graph node, maybe one per node or one for all; asks for research on the embedding model and whether data size matters.
decisions.change: Embeddings are fixed per index version and changed only by a planned re-index; the chat model is movable per graph role by config, with one model everywhere by default.

decisions.title: Model and provider per role
decisions.question: Which provider and model should each AI role use by default?
decisions.context: The agent has four AI roles: answering (chat model), screening input (guard classifier), turning text into vectors (embeddings) and re-sorting search results by relevance (reranker). Each can use a different provider. Costs are per million tokens; a typical chat turn here is about 5,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens. Prompt caching makes repeated prompt prefixes cheaper, but Haiku 4.5 only caches prefixes of at least 4,096 tokens.

options.label: Haiku 4.5 chat and guard, voyage-4-lite embeddings, rerank-2.5-lite
options.description: About USD 0.0075 per turn; embeddings and reranking inside Voyage's free 200M tokens; OpenAI adapters as the tested alternative; confirmed by an eval experiment.
pros: Free embeddings at this corpus size
One vendor for embeddings and reranking
cons: Haiku's cache minimum needs a stable owner brief in the prompt to benefit

options.label: OpenAI for everything (GPT-5.4-mini, text-embedding-3-small)
options.description: One vendor for all roles.
cons: No reranker from the same vendor

options.label: Sonnet 5.5 for chat
options.description: A stronger model for answers.
cons: About twice the cost per turn

decisions.why: It fits the Haiku-class budget, handles es, en and de well, and costs almost nothing for retrieval; the provider-agnostic layer means an eval can overturn it with a config change.
decisions.learn: Embeddings, reranking, prompt caching, cost per turn, model evaluation.
decisions.ownerNote: Haiku as the base, but switching to Sonnet 5.5 or an OpenAI model must be possible; asks which parts should be movable and which fixed, for simplicity.
decisions.change: Haiku 4.5 is the default for every role; per-role overrides (Sonnet 5.5, an OpenAI model) are adopted only after an eval experiment; the fixed and movable parts are listed in ADR-014.

decisions.title: Agent graph shape
decisions.question: How should the agent's LangGraph graph be structured?
decisions.context: A workflow is a fixed path you code; an agent is a loop where the model decides which tool to call next. LangGraph lets you mix both: deterministic nodes for steps you always want (guards, retrieval, checks) and a bounded tool-calling loop where the model needs to decide. Putting safety in code nodes instead of the prompt makes it testable and impossible for the model to skip.

options.label: Custom StateGraph, retrieve first, bounded tool subgraph
options.description: Preflight, input guard, retrieval, a small tool-calling agent with call limits, citation check, output guard, usage record.
pros: One fewer model round trip per turn
cons: More code than the prebuilt agent

options.label: Prebuilt createAgent (ReAct) with middleware
options.description: The model decides when to search or refuse.
cons: Safety depends on prompt and middleware order

options.label: Fixed workflow only
options.description: Guard, retrieve, answer, check with no tool loop.
cons: No follow-up lookups for multi-part questions

decisions.why: Deterministic guard and retrieval nodes make the agent safe and cheap by construction, while the bounded loop still handles questions that need a second lookup.
decisions.learn: Workflow vs agent, router, guard node, ReAct loop, corrective RAG, circuit breaker.
decisions.ownerNote: Prefers to build the StateGraph personally with AI assistance, to understand each part and how they connect.

decisions.title: RAG pipeline details
decisions.question: How should content be chunked, stored and retrieved for the agent?
decisions.context: Retrieval-augmented generation finds the content most relevant to a question and gives it to the model to answer from. Vector search finds passages with similar meaning; full-text search finds exact words and names; Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges the two ranked lists without comparing their incompatible scores. A reranker then reorders the top candidates by reading them against the question.

options.label: Structure-aware chunks, hybrid search + RRF + rerank, pgvector
options.description: One chunk per structured item, headings for long text, deterministic contextual headers; vector + full-text in Postgres fused with RRF; rerank top 20 to 5.
pros: Finds both meaning and exact names
cons: More moving parts than vector-only search

options.label: Vector-only search
options.description: Embeddings and nearest neighbors only.
cons: Misses exact names, versions and acronyms

options.label: Dedicated vector database (Qdrant)
options.description: A separate service for vectors.
cons: Another service and RAM for a corpus of a few hundred chunks

options.label: pgvector now, a Qdrant adapter later, decided by evals
options.description: Launch on option a; after launch implement KnowledgeIndexPort on Qdrant (hybrid Query API with RRF, collection aliases for re-index) and adopt it only if it beats pgvector on recall, MRR and latency.
pros: Learns a dedicated vector engine without risking launch
Uses the port for what it is for
cons: A second store while both run

decisions.why: Recommendation changed from a to d after the owner's note (F-6): pgvector stays the launch store, and a Qdrant adapter behind the same port lets the evals decide, which teaches the vector engine without risking launch.
decisions.learn: Embeddings, chunking, HNSW, full-text search, Reciprocal Rank Fusion, reranking.
decisions.ownerNote: a seems fine, but Qdrant is interesting to learn, though maybe overkill; worth exploring if the server supports it, to broaden the stack.
decisions.previousWhy: Hybrid search with fusion is the reliable default for a small, name-heavy corpus, and pgvector keeps everything in one database the agent already owns.
decisions.change: pgvector is the index for R2. WP-54 (R7) adds a Qdrant adapter behind KnowledgeIndexPort, capped at 512 MB, measured with the same retrieval evals (recall@5, MRR, latency); adopted only if it wins. The semantic cache (D-69) stays in pgvector unless Qdrant replaces the index, then it moves in the same step.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: pgvector only (a), or pgvector now plus a Qdrant adapter after launch, decided by evals (d)?

decisions.title: Conversation state and streaming
decisions.question: How should chat threads be remembered and answers streamed to the browser?
decisions.context: A LangGraph checkpointer saves the conversation state after every step, keyed by a thread id, so the next message continues the same thread. Server-Sent Events stream tokens one way from server to browser over plain HTTP. An output check that runs after generation cannot un-show streamed text, so checks must also run on the stream itself.

options.label: PostgresSaver, anonymous 24 h threads, SSE with incremental output checks
options.description: Thread id in a signed cookie, purge after 24 hours, stream tokens and abort if a check trips.
cons: Incremental checks are more complex than a final check

options.label: Buffer the full answer, then send JSON
options.description: Generate, check, then send.

options.label: WebSockets
options.description: Two-way connection.
cons: More moving parts than needed for request and response chat

decisions.why: Streaming feels fast and is safe here because nothing secret is ever in the model's context; the checks still abort a stream on a hit.
decisions.learn: Checkpointing, Server-Sent Events, streaming vs post-hoc checks.
decisions.ownerNote: Has always used b and wants to learn a if it is better; asks whether stored conversations should be encrypted for privacy.
decisions.change: Checkpoint payloads encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM through a custom serializer and a rotatable key; 24-hour purge; checkpoints left out of off-site backups. Second pass (2026-10-03): the encryption moves out of WP-22 into optional WP-56 (R7), because the key would live on the same server as the database and the real privacy controls are the 24-hour purge, the backup exclusion and LangSmith masking; WP-22 stays focused on the graph.

decisions.title: Where MCP is used
decisions.question: Where should the Model Context Protocol be used?
decisions.context: MCP is a standard protocol so any AI client (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, an IDE) can use tools and resources from any server, across process and vendor boundaries. Inside one service, tools are just functions; calling them over MCP only adds a network hop. A public MCP server lets anyone connect their own AI client to ask about the owner.

options.label: Public read-only MCP server later; none inside the agent
options.description: An mcp process type of the agent service on mcp.jadero.dev, after launch.
pros: A real, demonstrable integration any AI client can use
cons: One more public surface to rate-limit

options.label: The site agent calls its own tools over MCP
options.description: Expose tools on an MCP server and load them with the MCP adapters.
cons: Network hop and new failure modes for no user value

options.label: No MCP
options.description: Skip it.

decisions.why: MCP adds value where it crosses a boundary to other people's clients; inside the agent it would only add latency and failure modes. Timing superseded by D-58: the owner approved the public MCP at launch (WP-36).
decisions.learn: MCP tools, resources, transports; driving adapters.
decisions.ownerNote: Yes: an MCP that anyone, colleagues included, can use from Claude to ask about the owner's experience without the site's agent.

decisions.title: Default locale
decisions.question: Which language should the site show when nothing else is known?
decisions.context: The site has es, en and de. The default applies when the browser's Accept-Language header matches none of them, and the visitor's choice is remembered in a cookie. The audience is international: engineering teams and recruiters inside and outside the current employer, where English is the common working language.

options.label: English, with detection and a remembered choice
options.description: Default en; Accept-Language picks es or de when it matches.
cons: Spanish-first visitors land on English if their browser says so

options.label: Spanish
options.description: Default es.
cons: Less natural for an international team

decisions.why: English serves the widest professional audience; detection still gives Spanish and German speakers their language.

decisions.title: Locales required to publish
decisions.question: Which translations must exist before an item can be published?
decisions.context: Every content item has a translation per locale. Requiring all three slows publishing; requiring none risks half-translated pages. The admin shows completeness per locale either way.

options.label: en and es required, de warned
options.description: Publishing needs English and Spanish; German shows a warning until complete.
pros: Keeps the two strongest languages complete

options.label: All three required
options.description: No publish without es, en and de.

options.label: Only en required
options.description: Other languages fall back to English.

decisions.why: Requiring the two languages the owner writes best keeps quality high without blocking on German, which can also get machine drafts later (WP-32).

decisions.title: LangSmith setup
decisions.question: How should agent tracing be configured?
decisions.context: LangSmith records every agent run as a trace: each node, model call, tool call, tokens and timing. The free Developer plan includes 5,000 base traces per month with 14-day retention, and EU data residency is available on every plan. Visitor messages are personal data, so tracing must appear in the privacy notice and unnecessary fields should be masked.

options.label: Tracing in staging and production, EU region, masking, free plan
options.description: One project per environment.
cons: Visitor text leaves the server (masked where possible)

options.label: Tracing in staging only
options.description: Production untraced.
cons: Blind to real-world failures and attacks

options.label: Self-hosted Langfuse instead
options.description: Open-source alternative on the box.

decisions.why: Production traces are where attacks and failures show up; the EU region and masking keep the privacy cost low.
decisions.learn: Tracing, spans, privacy by design.
decisions.ownerNote: Privacy is a concern; self-hosted Langfuse is interesting for learning but adds time and complexity, and the server may not cope.

decisions.title: Eval gates in CI
decisions.question: When should agent evaluations run, and what should block a merge?
decisions.context: Evals measure agent quality on fixed datasets: answers grounded in sources, valid citations, correct refusals on attacks. Unlike unit tests they cost money per run and are statistical. Gates turn the most important results into merge blockers.

options.label: Path-filtered PRs + nightly, budget per run, adversarial 100% gate
options.description: Run when agent, AI or prompt files change and every night; block on any adversarial regression or a drop in groundedness or recall.

options.label: Nightly only
options.description: No PR gating.

options.label: Manual runs
options.description: Run when someone remembers.

decisions.why: Security regressions in a public agent must never merge, and path filters keep the cost to the PRs that can cause them.
decisions.learn: Evals vs tests, LLM-as-judge, experiment baselines.
decisions.ownerNote: Start with a and try others if spend jumps; asks whether moving from a to b later is hard or just configuration.

decisions.title: Visual direction
decisions.question: Which visual direction should the site take?
decisions.context: Three directions were proposed: terminal editorial (developer-native, monospace accents, a command-palette agent prompt), Swiss editorial (calm, large serif headings, generous whitespace) and bento glass (bento-grid cards, soft gradients, glass surfaces). All share Tailwind v4 tokens, shadcn/ui, light and dark modes and accessibility targets. WP-15 builds three throwaway hero mockups so the choice is made from screenshots.

options.label: Swiss editorial base + terminal-style agent prompt
options.description: An editorial base that reads as credible to any engineering audience, with the terminal-style ask-me prompt as one memorable interactive element.

options.label: Terminal editorial
options.description: Developer-native throughout.
cons: Frames the whole site around the agent

options.label: Bento glass
options.description: Contemporary and showy.
cons: Glass contrast is hard in light mode

decisions.why: The editorial base reads as senior and credible to any engineering audience, and the terminal-style prompt adds one memorable interaction without making the agent the whole story; the final call comes from the mockups.

decisions.title: PDF CV generation
decisions.question: How should the per-language PDF CV be produced?
decisions.context: The CV must come from the same content as the site, in three languages, and refresh when content is published. Rendering can use a React-to-PDF library in Node, a headless browser printing a web page, or a typesetting tool.

options.label: react-pdf in api-worker, regenerated on publish
options.description: A packages/cv template fed by the content data.
cons: A separate template from the web page design

options.label: Playwright printing a CV page
options.description: Headless Chromium prints a print-styled route.
cons: Chromium adds hundreds of MB to an image

options.label: Typst template
options.description: Typesetting from JSON.

decisions.why: react-pdf runs in the existing worker process without a browser, which matters on an 8 GB server.

decisions.title: Guard architecture
decisions.question: How should the agent be protected against prompt injection, jailbreaks and prompt leaks?
decisions.context: Prompt injection is text that tries to override the agent's instructions, directly from a visitor or hidden in content it reads. Defense in depth stacks independent layers: deterministic input rules, a classifier, safe handling of retrieved content, read-only tools, output checks and monitoring. The most mature guardrail libraries are Python; in TypeScript, LangChain's middleware is the most mature surface.

options.label: Own guard module + LangChain middleware
options.description: Rules plus a swappable classifier (Haiku first, local Prompt Guard 2 as an eval-decided experiment), canary token and output checks.

options.label: Adopt a young TS guard library
options.description: Use an npm guard package as the main layer.
cons: Young projects on a security-critical path

options.label: Python sidecar (LLM Guard or NeMo)
options.description: A Python service with scanners; LLM Guard was archived in July 2026, NeMo Guardrails and Prompt Guard 2 remain.
cons: A second language and its models on the box
LLM Guard is no longer maintained

options.label: Hosted guard API (Lakera)
options.description: Send messages to a guard service.

options.label: TypeScript guard now, Python classifier service later
options.description: Launch with option a; after launch add a FastAPI service running Prompt Guard 2 as a second GuardClassifierPort adapter, behind a timeout and a circuit breaker that falls back to the Haiku classifier; evals pick the winner.
pros: Real Python in a contained piece
The chat never depends on it

decisions.why: Recommendation changed from a to e after the owner's note (F-7): LLM Guard was archived in July 2026, so the Python piece is a Prompt Guard 2 classifier service behind the existing port, added after launch with a fallback, so the chat never depends on it.
decisions.learn: OWASP LLM Top 10 2025, defense in depth, canary tokens, untrusted-content policy.
decisions.ownerNote: Open to Python to try another language, since the agentic team uses it a lot; wants the pros and cons of building everything vs using a Python library.
decisions.previousWhy: Building the layers teaches each defense and keeps them testable; libraries and datasets still feed rules and test cases.
decisions.change: TypeScript guard module with the Haiku classifier in R2 (WP-23). WP-55 (R7) adds a small Python service (FastAPI + Prompt Guard 2 86M) as a second adapter behind GuardClassifierPort, called with a timeout and a circuit breaker that falls back to Haiku; the evals decide which adapter stays. Recorded as a deliberate exception to the brainstorm's TypeScript-everywhere rule: Python enters where it is strongest (running a model) and the chat never depends on it. It replaces the Prompt Guard 2 ONNX-in-Node experiment.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: Keep the TypeScript guard only (a), or add a Python Prompt Guard 2 classifier service after launch behind the same port (e)?

decisions.title: Rate-limit storage
decisions.question: Where should rate-limit counters be stored?
decisions.context: Rate limiting counts requests per client in a time window and rejects the excess. In-memory counters reset on every deploy; a shared store survives restarts. Each service should keep its own counters so services stay independent.

options.label: Throttler with custom Postgres storage per service
options.description: Counters in an unlogged table in each service's own database.

options.label: In-memory
options.description: The throttler default.

options.label: Valkey or Redis
options.description: A key-value store for counters.

decisions.why: Postgres is already there, survives deploys and keeps each service's limits in its own data.
decisions.learn: Fixed window, sliding window, token bucket.

decisions.title: Limit values
decisions.question: What starting limits should protect the agent and the budget?
decisions.context: Limits bound abuse at every scale: per request (input and output size), per thread, per IP per minute and per day, per day in the app, and per month at the provider. The app-level daily cap must trip before the provider's monthly limit, which cuts traffic without warning.

options.label: Proposed values
options.description: 6 per minute and 40 per day per IP; 12 messages per thread; 500 characters in; 600 tokens out; USD 1.50 per day in the app; USD 20 per month at the provider.
pros: Worst case is bounded and small

options.label: Looser values
options.description: Double every limit.

options.label: Stricter values
options.description: Halve every limit.

decisions.why: These numbers keep the worst month to a few tens of dollars while leaving room for real conversations; tune them from the usage dashboard.
decisions.learn: Unbounded consumption (LLM10), circuit breaker.

decisions.title: Bot protection
decisions.question: How should bots be kept away from the chat and the contact form?
decisions.context: A challenge widget proves a visitor is probably human; the token is verified server-side. A honeypot is a hidden form field that humans leave empty and bots fill. The old site used Google reCAPTCHA.

options.label: Cloudflare Turnstile + honeypot on the form
options.description: Turnstile once per chat session and on the contact form.

options.label: Google reCAPTCHA v3
options.description: Score-based, familiar from the old site.

options.label: Honeypot and timing only
options.description: No third party.

decisions.why: Turnstile gives strong protection without tracking concerns, and the honeypot adds a free extra layer on the form.
decisions.learn: Bot mitigation, server-side token verification.

decisions.title: Repository visibility
decisions.question: Should the repository be public at launch?
decisions.context: On GitHub Free, deployment environments, environment secrets and required reviewers only work on public repositories, and CodeQL code scanning is free for public repositories. A public repo also lets reviewers read the code the site talks about. The risk is leaking secrets in history, which a gitleaks scan of the full history checks before going public.

options.label: Public before launch, after a gitleaks history scan
options.description: Develop private, scan, then flip.

options.label: Stay private
options.description: Repo-level secrets and an owner-only manual production deploy.
cons: No environment approvals or environment secrets on Free

options.label: Private on a paid plan
options.description: Pay for environment features.
cons: Required reviewers for private repos still need Enterprise

decisions.why: A portfolio repo gains far more from being readable than it risks, and going public unlocks the deployment safety features for free.
decisions.learn: Supply chain hygiene, secret scanning.

decisions.title: Staging after cutover
decisions.question: What happens to the staging environment once jadero.dev switches to v2?
decisions.context: During the build, new.jadero.dev is where everything runs first. After cutover, a staging environment still lets releases be checked before production, but running it permanently costs about 1.6 GB of RAM on an 8 GB server.

options.label: Keep as staging.jadero.dev, stopped by default
options.description: The deploy workflow starts it when a release goes to staging.
cons: A few seconds of start-up per staging deploy

options.label: Always-on staging
options.description: Runs permanently.
cons: About 1.6 GB of RAM all the time

options.label: No staging after cutover
options.description: Deploy straight to production.
cons: No place to catch a bad release

decisions.why: Keeping staging but stopped keeps the safety net without paying for it in memory.

decisions.title: External uptime check
decisions.question: Should something outside the server check that the site is up?
decisions.context: Uptime Kuma runs on the same server it monitors, so if the server itself goes down it cannot send the alert. A free hosted check from outside covers that blind spot.

options.label: Yes, one free external check
options.description: A hosted ping on the home page and the API health.
pros: Alerts even when the box is down

options.label: No, Uptime Kuma only
options.description: Self-monitoring only.

decisions.why: A monitor that dies with the thing it monitors cannot report that failure; one free external check fixes it.

decisions.title: Deploy access to the server
decisions.question: How should GitHub Actions reach the server to deploy?
decisions.context: Deploying needs some way in. GitHub's runners have changing IP addresses, so a public SSH port must be open to the whole internet. Tailscale puts the runner and the server on a private network, so the public SSH port can close. A forced command restricts a key to running one script instead of a shell.

options.label: SSH over Tailscale with a forced-command key
options.description: Port 22 closed publicly; the key can only run the deploy script.
pros: A stolen key cannot open a shell
cons: One more account and auth key to rotate

options.label: SSH to a public port 22
options.description: Key-only SSH open to the internet.

options.label: Pull-based deploy
options.description: A process on the server polls for new images.
cons: Weaker control of migrations and rollbacks

decisions.why: It removes the public SSH surface entirely and limits what the deploy key can do, at the cost of one Tailscale setup.
decisions.learn: Least privilege, forced commands, zero-trust networking.

decisions.title: Portfolio content inventory
decisions.question: Which projects appear, and how are the brainstorm and the code triage reconciled?
decisions.context: The brainstorm listed projects from memory; the later triage read the code and marked several as course copies. Presenting course work as original work hurts credibility with technical reviewers. confluence-agent was work for the current employer, so it is not a personal project.

options.label: Follow the triage
options.description: Drop Nest-Microservices from selected projects; Teslo-shop and the-wild-oasis only in the early archive labeled as course work; confluence-agent at most as an owner-approved public-level bullet under the current role.
pros: Every claim survives a code read

options.label: Keep the brainstorm list
options.description: Show every project named in the brainstorm.
cons: Course copies presented as selected work

decisions.why: A shorter list of honest, code-backed projects reads better to any technical reviewer than a longer list that includes course copies.

decisions.title: Agent tooling for the repo
decisions.question: Should the repo use the owner's Claude Code framework or its own agent setup?
decisions.context: The owner's framework brings a governed flow (plan, approve, per-work-package implementation, review gate) and guard hooks, but it is one bundle today with company-specific skills, and its ADRs are untracked. This project needs tracked ADRs, GitHub delivery and a learning gate the framework does not have. A core-plugin and company-pack split is planned but not done.

options.label: Repo-local setup now, framework core plugin later
options.description: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, a few skills and a learning-gate hook, named to map onto the framework's concepts.
cons: Re-creates a few guards the framework has

options.label: Install the framework as it is
options.description: Use the whole bundle.
cons: Company content in a personal repo
Flow too heavy for a learning project

options.label: Wait for the core plugin
options.description: Use core plugin + jadero-dev pack when it exists.

decisions.why: It unblocks the build today, keeps the personal repo free of company material, and can adopt the core plugin later if it adds mechanical value.
decisions.learn: Agent instructions, hooks as mechanism, learning gate.

decisions.title: Lint, format and architecture checks
decisions.question: Which tools should format code and enforce architecture rules?
decisions.context: A formatter and linter keep style consistent and catch common mistakes. Architecture fitness functions are automated checks that the intended structure holds, for example that domain code never imports infrastructure, or that one app never imports another. commitlint enforces conventional commit messages, which the release tooling reads.

options.label: Biome + dependency-cruiser + commitlint
options.description: Biome for format and lint, dependency-cruiser for architecture rules, commitlint on commits and PR titles.

options.label: ESLint + Prettier + dependency-cruiser
options.description: The classic stack.

decisions.why: Biome is simpler and faster, and the rules that matter most (architecture) come from dependency-cruiser either way.
decisions.learn: Architecture fitness functions, conventional commits.

decisions.title: Versioning and releases
decisions.question: How should versions and changelogs be produced?
decisions.context: Conventional commits (feat, fix, feat!) can drive version numbers automatically: a fix bumps the patch, a feature the minor, a breaking change the major. With services, each one should be able to release and deploy on its own, which means its own version line. release-please keeps a Release PR open; merging it is the deliberate ship moment.

options.label: release-please, one component per service
options.description: Own version, changelog and tag per service; shared package releases bump their consumers.
cons: More tags and changelogs to read

options.label: release-please, one product version
options.description: One version for everything.

options.label: semantic-release
options.description: Releases automatically on every qualifying push.

options.label: Changesets
options.description: Hand-written change files per package.

decisions.why: Per-service versions are what makes the services genuinely independent, and the Release PR keeps the owner in control of when things ship.
decisions.learn: Semantic versioning, conventional commits, release trains vs independent releases.

decisions.title: Contact form
decisions.question: Should v1 include a contact form, and how?
decisions.context: The old site had a contact form with reCAPTCHA. Store-and-forward means the form first saves the message, answers the visitor right away, and sends the notification email later from a queue, so a mail outage never loses a message. Auto-replies to the address a visitor types turn a form into a spam relay.

options.label: A contact service in v1
options.description: Form, bot check, store-and-forward with an outbox, notification to the owner only, retries and dead letters.
pros: The best first microservice to learn on

options.label: No form; email and LinkedIn links
options.description: The previous recommendation.
cons: Misses the owner's request and a learning vehicle

options.label: A form endpoint inside api
options.description: Same flow, no separate service.
cons: A mail or spam problem shares a process with content

decisions.why: It is small enough to finish quickly and exercises every messaging pattern before the agent depends on them.
decisions.learn: Store-and-forward, asynchronous request-reply (202 Accepted), spam relay.

decisions.title: How learning work packages run
decisions.question: How should a learning work package be executed so the owner learns each step?
decisions.context: The owner wants to understand every backend and agent step, not just approve results. A learning gate means no code lands in a learning area until an explainer exists and the owner has made the decision it asks for. Explaining back in your own words is the quickest test of real understanding.

options.label: Explainer, decision gate, small visible steps, explain-back
options.description: Concepts and a concrete trace first, owner decides, then implementation in small steps in the main session, then a recap.
pros: The owner sees and understands every step

options.label: Delegated implementation with a summary
options.description: Agents build; the owner reads a summary.

decisions.why: Learning is a hard requirement, and the gate turns it into a mechanism instead of a good intention.
decisions.learn: Learning gate, explain-back, concrete traces.
decisions.ownerNote: Find the balance between learning and speed; topics the owner already knows can go straight to implementation.
decisions.change: Adds a fast path: a WP or step marked known needs only the decision record; the full explainer and explain-back stay for new material.

decisions.title: Service boundaries
decisions.question: How far should the system be split into services?
decisions.context: Services buy independent failure, deploys and resource limits; they cost network failures, eventual consistency, contracts and more operations. A boundary pays when a part fails differently, changes on its own rhythm, has a different security exposure, or does slow work that must not block others. The distributed monolith is the trap: services that share data or call each other synchronously all the time, so you pay for distribution without getting independence.

options.label: Modular monolith + extracted services where isolation pays
options.description: api (content, auth), agent (+ agent-ingest), contact; background work as process types; web and a static admin.
pros: Isolation where failures actually come from

options.label: Pure modular monolith
options.description: One NestJS app (the previous recommendation).
cons: An agent crash takes content down

options.label: Full microservices
options.description: One service per module plus a gateway.

decisions.why: It gives the owner the isolation they asked for exactly where it matters (agent and contact), keeps strongly related modules together, and avoids the distributed-monolith trap.
decisions.learn: Bounded context, database per service, process types, distributed monolith.

decisions.title: Message broker
decisions.question: Which broker should carry messages between services?
decisions.context: A broker accepts messages from producers and delivers them to consumers, keeping them safe if a consumer is down. RabbitMQ routes messages through exchanges to queues by binding rules, which suits fanning one event out to several services. Log-based systems such as Kafka keep an ordered history and suit high-volume streaming.

options.label: RabbitMQ 4
options.description: Topic exchange, durable quorum queues, dead-letter exchanges, TTL retry tiers, vhosts per environment.
pros: The owner meets it at work

options.label: NATS + JetStream
options.description: Lightweight messaging with a persistence layer.
cons: Nest's built-in transport is fire and forget

options.label: Redis Streams (Valkey)
options.description: Append-only log with consumer groups.
cons: Retries and dead letters are do-it-yourself

options.label: pg-boss
options.description: A queue inside Postgres.

decisions.why: RabbitMQ's routing and dead-letter features fit this event flow, the memory cost is affordable, and the knowledge transfers to the owner's work.
decisions.learn: Exchanges, bindings, quorum queues, acknowledgments, prefetch, dead-letter exchange.
decisions.ownerNote: Wants to learn RabbitMQ.

decisions.title: RabbitMQ client in NestJS
decisions.question: Which library should services use to talk to RabbitMQ?
decisions.context: Nest's built-in RabbitMQ transport only uses RabbitMQ's default exchange and wraps every message in a fixed pattern and data format, which hides the topology the owner wants to learn and makes topic routing awkward. Community modules expose exchanges and routing keys directly. Either way, the library sits behind our own MessageBus port so it can be swapped.

options.label: @golevelup/nestjs-rabbitmq behind our port
options.description: Decorators for subscribing with exchange, routing key and queue.

options.label: Own adapter over amqplib
options.description: A thin adapter written in the messaging package.

options.label: Nest's built-in RMQ transport
options.description: The official microservices transport.

decisions.why: It exposes the real RabbitMQ model with little code; the own amqplib adapter is the fallback if Nest 12 support lags.
decisions.ownerNote: An adapter would allow swapping RabbitMQ for another broker; unsure it is worth it beyond learning.

decisions.title: How the agent gets content
decisions.question: Should the agent call the content API, or keep its own copy of the content?
decisions.context: If the agent calls api synchronously for every lookup, an api outage breaks the chat: a hidden coupling. Event-carried state transfer means each content.published event carries the full published item, and the agent stores it in its own read model. The agent then answers from its own data, a few seconds behind the latest publish. The copy is a derived search index (chunks and vectors), not a second source of truth: api keeps the entries, revisions and approval state that the site and the admin need.

options.label: Own read model fed by events
options.description: agent-ingest stores published content and indexes it; tools read locally.
pros: Chat works while api is down
cons: Seconds of lag after a publish
A derived index next to the source (rebuildable from events)

options.label: Synchronous calls to api with a circuit breaker
options.description: Tools call api; the breaker fails fast when it is down.
cons: Chat degrades whenever api is down

options.label: The agent owns knowledge entries end to end
options.description: Entries, revisions and approval live in agent; api keeps the CV, projects and posts.
pros: One owner for everything the agent reads
cons: The agent becomes a content service too
An agent outage stops entry editing and work-log pages

decisions.why: Confirmed by the owner after the explanation (F-8): api owns the content (source of truth: entries, revisions, approval state); agent owns a search index derived from it (chunks, embeddings, full-text), rebuildable from api's events at any time. This is a CQRS read model, not a second copy of the same thing: api never sees a vector and agent never edits content.
decisions.learn: Event-carried state transfer, read model, CQRS-style separation.
decisions.ownerNote: Asks why data is stored twice: the agent's data is what lives in the vector database for RAG and api should not know about it; does not see the duplication or the api and agent split.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: With the copy explained as a derived search index, confirm a, or choose c (the agent owns knowledge entries)?

decisions.title: Message contracts
decisions.question: How should message formats be defined and checked?
decisions.context: Every message needs an id (for deduplication), a type with a version, and trace context. CloudEvents is a standard envelope for exactly that. AsyncAPI documents message channels the way OpenAPI documents HTTP, and contract tests make each consumer parse the producer's example messages in CI.

options.label: CloudEvents + Zod + AsyncAPI + fixture contract tests
options.description: Envelope standard, Zod schemas in packages/contracts, an AsyncAPI catalog, consumer tests against producer fixtures.

options.label: Ad hoc JSON
options.description: Each service shapes its own messages.

options.label: Protobuf or Avro with a schema registry
options.description: Binary schemas and a registry service.

options.label: Pact consumer-driven contracts
options.description: A contract broker and verification flow.
cons: Heavier than needed inside one monorepo

decisions.why: Zod is already the project's schema language, and fixture tests in one monorepo give the same safety as heavier tools with far less setup.
decisions.learn: CloudEvents, AsyncAPI, schema evolution, consumer-driven contracts.
decisions.ownerNote: Asks whether a separate toolbox repository publishing versioned packages (types, contracts, schemas) would avoid duplication across services.

decisions.title: Admin delivery
decisions.question: Where and how should the admin interface run?
decisions.context: The admin is used by one person a few times a week, behind a login. A static single-page app is just files: nothing runs on the server, so nothing can crash or leak memory. Keeping it on its own subdomain gives it its own security policy and keeps admin code out of the public site.

options.label: Static SPA on admin.jadero.dev
options.description: Vite + React + shadcn/ui, built to files that nginx serves.
cons: No server rendering (not needed behind a login)

options.label: Separate Next.js app
options.description: A second Next app on the admin subdomain.
cons: About 250 MB RAM for a rarely used tool

options.label: /admin inside web
options.description: The original plan.
cons: Shares the public app's failures and attack surface

decisions.why: A static SPA costs nothing to run and isolates the privileged UI completely from the public site.
decisions.learn: Static hosting, Content Security Policy, attack surface.

decisions.title: Edge gateway
decisions.question: Should a gateway component sit in front of the services?
decisions.context: A gateway is the single entry point that routes requests and applies cross-cutting rules. The host nginx can route by path, cache pages, rate-limit and check admin sessions through auth_request, and with proxy_cache_use_stale it keeps serving the last good page if the web app is down.

options.label: Host nginx as the gateway
options.description: Routing, TLS, rate limits, auth_request and a stale-serving page cache.
pros: Keeps the site up when web is down

options.label: Traefik
options.description: Docker-label-driven routing.

options.label: NestJS gateway service
options.description: A Nest app proxying all traffic.
cons: A new shared point of failure

options.label: nginx at the edge plus a thin NestJS gateway
options.description: nginx keeps TLS, static files, the stale page cache and coarse limits; a NestJS gateway behind it handles /api/* only: routing, admin session check, correlation ids, per-route limits, merged OpenAPI docs, SSE pass-through. No business logic, no database.
pros: Learns the gateway pattern in tested TypeScript
One place for API cross-cutting rules
cons: One more hop and about 150 MB
A new single point of failure for /api/*

decisions.why: The owner wants to learn the gateway pattern; the plan's own warning (a gateway every call crosses is a new shared point of failure) is respected by building it after the site is live and keeping nginx's stale cache in front of it.
decisions.learn: Gateway offloading, gateway routing, backends for frontends, reverse proxy caching, streaming through a proxy.
decisions.ownerNote: A NestJS gateway service appeals for learning even as another point of failure; unsure despite picking a; the question repeats D-2; wants the best of both; suggests firstmate study the employer's gateway for patterns only.
decisions.previousWhy: nginx already covers every gateway job, and the stale cache adds real resilience for free.
decisions.change: Phased (second pass, F-1): nginx alone is the edge through R0 and R1, so the walking skeleton and the first production release carry no extra hop. The thin NestJS gateway is built as learning WP-53 in R7, after the site is in production, with an entry rule: it takes on only what nginx cannot do (admin session check in tested TypeScript, merged OpenAPI document, an admin backend-for-frontend); per-route API limits move to it and nginx keeps only coarse limits, so limits are never enforced twice. Pages and static files never pass through it.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: nginx only (a), or nginx at the edge plus a thin NestJS gateway for the API routes (d)?

decisions.title: Mail provider
decisions.question: Which provider should send the contact notifications?
decisions.context: Hetzner blocks outbound ports 25 and 465 on new cloud servers, so mail must go through a provider's HTTPS API or SMTP submission on port 587. Volume is tiny: a few notifications a week, only to the owner.

options.label: Resend behind MailPort
options.description: Free tier of 3,000 emails per month, 100 per day; simple API; a fake adapter for tests.
cons: Domain DNS records to set up

options.label: Postmark
options.description: Free developer plan of 100 emails per month.

options.label: SMTP on port 587 via an existing mailbox
options.description: Use the owner's mail account.

decisions.why: Resend's free tier and API are more than enough, and the MailPort keeps Postmark one adapter away.

decisions.title: Admin authorization across services
decisions.question: How do agent and contact know an admin request comes from the owner?
decisions.context: Sessions live in api. With nginx auth_request, nginx asks api whether the session is valid before forwarding any admin request, and passes a signed identity header to the target service. That keeps all authentication code in one place.

options.label: nginx auth_request + signed internal header
options.description: One decision point at the edge; services only verify the header signature.
pros: No auth code in other services
No synchronous auth calls between services
cons: One internal hop per admin request

options.label: Each service calls api to validate the session
options.description: A synchronous check per admin request.

options.label: Short-lived JWTs verified locally
options.description: api issues tokens; services verify signatures.

options.label: The gateway verifies the session and forwards a signed identity
options.description: With the D-45 hybrid, the NestJS gateway checks the session against api (cached about 30 s), strips identity headers that came from outside and forwards a signed, timestamped header the services verify.
pros: Still one decision point and no auth code in other services
cons: Only applies if D-45 is d
The gateway calls api to validate (cached)

decisions.why: Recommendation follows D-45 (F-3): with the gateway, the single decision point moves from nginx config into gateway code; if D-45 stays a, option a remains the choice.
decisions.learn: Gateway authentication, trust boundaries.
decisions.ownerNote: Asks what would change with the NestJS gateway, or with both nginx and the gateway.
decisions.previousWhy: It centralizes the security decision at the edge and keeps the services free of auth logic and of runtime dependencies on api.
decisions.change: a now, d later (F-3): nginx auth_request to api with a signed identity header through R6. The header is an HMAC with an internal key and a timestamp from the start, so a captured header expires. When WP-53 lands (R7), the session check moves into the gateway (option d) and nginx stops running auth_request; the services verify the header exactly as before.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: Follows D-45: a gateway session check (d) if D-45 is d, otherwise nginx auth_request (a).

decisions.title: Database isolation
decisions.question: How should each service's data be separated?
decisions.context: Database per service means no service can read another's tables, so they can only couple through published contracts. Isolation can be a separate schema, a separate database, or a separate server; on one 8 GB box, a separate Postgres instance per service would waste memory.

options.label: One instance, one database and role per service
options.description: Each role can connect only to its own database.
pros: One instance to run and back up
cons: Postgres remains a shared point of failure

options.label: One database, one schema per service
options.description: Separate schemas and roles in one database.
cons: Easier to cross the line by accident

options.label: One Postgres instance per service
options.description: Separate containers.
cons: Memory multiplied on a small server

decisions.why: Separate databases make the boundary enforced by Postgres itself, while one instance keeps memory and backups simple.
decisions.learn: Database per service, least privilege.

decisions.title: Resilience policies
decisions.question: How should calls to external providers (AI, mail) handle failures?
decisions.context: A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency for a while, so requests fail fast instead of piling up. Retries with exponential backoff handle short blips, timeouts stop slow calls from hanging, and a bulkhead limits how many calls run at once so one slow provider cannot exhaust the process. These policies can be composed.

options.label: cockatiel
options.description: A TypeScript library of composable policies: retry, circuit breaker, timeout, bulkhead.
cons: API to verify at build time

options.label: opossum
options.description: A popular Node circuit-breaker library.
cons: Circuit breaker only; other policies separate

options.label: Hand-rolled
options.description: Write the policies ourselves.

decisions.why: Composable, typed policies cover every failure mode around providers with little code, and the concepts stay visible in the configuration.
decisions.learn: Circuit breaker, retry with backoff, timeout, bulkhead.
decisions.ownerNote: Unsure because composable policies are new to the owner; interesting to learn and to propose at work if they work well.

decisions.title: Content layers and the approval gate
decisions.question: How should the CV and the detailed knowledge behind it be modeled, and how is unapproved content kept out of the agent?
decisions.context: Layer A is the CV: short, curated bullets ordered by importance. Layer B is a knowledge base of detailed entries (problem, context, what was built, patterns, trade-offs, testing and rollout, outcome), each linked from the CV bullets it supports by a stable id. An approval state bound to a specific revision decides what the agent may read. Defense in depth means the gate is checked three times: the producer only emits events for approved revisions, the consumer rejects anything else, and a daily reconciliation removes anything that slipped through.

options.label: Two layers, structured entries, per-locale approval, gated indexing
options.description: CvBullet and KnowledgeEntry aggregates; approval per locale bound to a revision; approved and withdrawn events; consumer validation; daily reconciliation.
pros: Every CV claim can be drilled into with evidence
Structure feeds better answers about patterns and trade-offs
Drafts can never reach the index
cons: Many entries for the owner to write

options.label: Single layer
options.description: Projects, posts and experience items only.
cons: CV claims cannot be drilled into

options.label: Free-form posts with a private flag
options.description: Entries as Markdown posts; a boolean hides drafts.
cons: A flag is easier to flip by mistake than an approval bound to a revision

decisions.why: It turns the CV into a set of claims backed by evidence the visitor can explore, and the three-check gate makes leaking a draft a multi-bug event instead of a one-line mistake.
decisions.learn: Summary and evidence layers, approval state machine, tombstone events, anti-entropy reconciliation, defense in depth.
decisions.ownerNote: Not fully clear; the agent will hold far more detail than the CV in the vector database; documents could be one or several per topic (bugs, tech debt, performance) or one per big feature, to be decided.
decisions.change: Wording aligned with ADR-031: entries are English only, so approval is per entry (not per locale); topics such as tech debt or performance are filters on type, domain and patterns, not separate documents; a big feature becomes several entries linked through related.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: Confirm two layers with the approval gate (a), with entries per piece of work and topics as tags.

decisions.title: Knowledge-base chunking and retrieval
decisions.question: How should knowledge entries be chunked and retrieved so answers are both precise and complete?
decisions.context: Small chunks match questions precisely but lose surrounding context; big chunks keep context but blur the match. Parent-document (small-to-big) retrieval searches small chunks and then hands the model the whole parent document they came from. When a visitor clicks a specific CV bullet, the linked entries are already known, so they can be fetched by id with no search at all.

options.label: Section chunks + parent expansion + drill-down by id
options.description: One chunk per entry section with a contextual header; the top 1 to 3 parent entries go to the model whole; CV bullet clicks fetch linked entries directly.
cons: More retrieval logic to build and test

options.label: One chunk per entry
options.description: Embed each entry as a whole.
cons: A long entry's vector blurs its sections, weaker matching

options.label: Fixed-size token chunks
options.description: Split every entry every N tokens.

decisions.why: The entries are already structured into sections, so section chunks match well, parent expansion restores the full story, and drill-down by id makes the most common question path deterministic.
decisions.learn: Parent-document retrieval, contextual chunk headers, deterministic retrieval paths.
decisions.ownerNote: Not fully clear, but the owner likes the idea.

decisions.title: Visibility of approved knowledge entries
decisions.question: Should approved knowledge entries also be public pages on the site?
decisions.context: Anything the agent can read, a determined visitor can extract through conversation, so an approved entry is effectively public either way. Public pages give every citation a real link target and let reviewers browse the evidence directly. Search engines can be allowed or asked not to index those pages.

options.label: Public work-log pages, indexed
options.description: Each approved entry gets a page that citations link to.
cons: Detailed work stories are easy to find

options.label: Public pages, noindex
options.description: Same pages, hidden from search engines.

options.label: Agent-only
options.description: No pages; citations expand an inline snippet in the chat.

decisions.why: Approval already means public, so pages add transparency and citation targets at no extra risk; noindex is a fine variant if the owner prefers lower search visibility.
decisions.learn: Citations to stable ids, approved equals public.
decisions.ownerNote: Fine as long as no proprietary employer information is included.
decisions.change: The owner's condition is recorded on the decision: nothing proprietary from the employer may appear, which D-53 enforces (checklist, private denylist, public_names allowlist, importer checks). Work-log pages carry a per-entry indexable flag (default true) so an entry can be public but kept out of search engines.
decisions.resolvedQuestion: Confirm public work-log pages for approved entries (a), with no proprietary employer information.

decisions.title: Pre-approval sensitivity check
decisions.question: How should entries be checked for non-public employer details before approval?
decisions.context: Many entries describe work for the current employer, which must stay at a public level. A checklist makes the owner confirm each rule explicitly; a denylist scan catches internal names automatically, but the denylist must never be committed to the public repo because it would itself leak those names. An LLM review can flag risky sentences the denylist does not know.

options.label: Checklist + private denylist scan + optional LLM review
options.description: The denylist lives in the admin database; automated checks warn, the owner decides.
pros: The owner keeps the final call

options.label: Checklist only
options.description: Manual confirmation per entry.

options.label: LLM review decides
options.description: An LLM approves or rejects.
cons: A model cannot know what is internal

decisions.why: Layered checks catch the obvious leaks automatically while keeping the judgment, and the accountability, with the owner.
decisions.learn: Data classification, defense in depth, human in the loop.

decisions.title: Recruiter agent design
decisions.question: How should the agent analyze a pasted job description against the owner's experience?
decisions.context: A job description is long, untrusted text that may even contain instructions aimed at the agent. Structured extraction turns it into a list of requirements first; then the agent looks for evidence per requirement (map), and only then writes a fit summary (reduce). Honest gaps ("no evidence found") build more trust with a recruiter than a model that claims a perfect match.

options.label: Evidence per requirement with a cited fit matrix
